newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan urges Cyprus leaders to preach reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: Annan urges Cyprus leaders to preach reconciliation.

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan asked Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders on Tuesday to promote tolerance and reconciliation after threats against those trying to improve contacts between the two communities.

He also urged the two sides to make a renewed effort to reach agreement on measures to reduce tension along the ceasefire line across the island after the failure of a series of negotiations that began last October.

Annan's comments were contained in a report to the Security Council recommending a six-month renewal, until Dec. 31, of the 1,200-member U.N. Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP), deployed since 1964.

A government comprising both Greek and Turkish Cypriots broke down in 1963 and Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since 1974 when troops from Turkey took control of the north of the island in reaction to a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta ruling Greece.
Annan said he would inform the Security Council separately of preparations for talks between the leaders of the two communities, who have not met for nearly three years.

President Glafcos Clerides, representing the Greek Cypriots, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash were expected to meet in New York around July 9 to try to revive long-stalled negotiations on reuniting the island under a bi-communal, bi-zonal federation.

Referring to efforts by UNFICYP to improve the overall atmosphere through activities involving the two communities, Annan said it would be desirable if such contacts could take place without formality and on a regular basis.

"From time to time, those who promote or participate in bi-communal events encounter pressure and even threats within their own community, making their efforts all the more admirable," he said. "I urge the two leaders to send clear messages of tolerance and reconciliation to their publics and to facilitate and encourage direct contacts between the two sides."

Regretting that there had been no change in the "excessive levels of military forces and armaments in Cyprus and the rate at which they are being expanded, upgraded and modernised," he said the military authorities had also not accepted a package of reciprocal measures proposed by UNFICYP to reduce tension along the ceasefire lines.
"Despite a total of 40 meetings with both sides at the chief of staff level, progress has not been possible," Annan said.

He was referring to such proposals as unmannning all areas where troops of the two sides are in close proximity, prohibiting loaded weapons along the ceasefire lines and adopting a code of conduct based based on minimum use of force.
"I strongly urge both sides to reconsider their positions and cooperate with UNFICYP to reach an agreement on this package without further delay," Annan said.
